clue.text: Clown had to be funny during smack, though reaction suggesting otherwise?

indicators.note: the scrambled letters sit during, that is inside, the word for smack

parts.note: a smack is a slap

indicators.note: to be funny the letters of the two words must be played about with and rearranged

explanation.surface: A clown has been told to be funny while being hit, though the audience reaction suggests it is not working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be funny' rearranges CLOWN HAD into OWHANDC, and 'during' puts that inside SLAP. The definition plays on the clown: a slow handclap tells a performer he is not funny at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A slow handclap is the audience's sarcastic applause, a reaction signalling boredom or disapproval rather than delight.

clue.text: Hint of Saatchi and Saatchi product, depravity

parts.note: Saatchi and Saatchi is a famous advertising agency, whose product is an ad
depravity is vice

explanation.surface: A clue to the moral corruption behind an advertising agency's output.
explanation.walkthrough: Saatchi and Saatchi is a well-known London advertising agency, so its product is an AD.
explanation.definitionFit: Advice is guidance or a suggestion, and a hint is a light piece of guidance, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Middle of city centre scrapped in redevelopment, possibly?

definitions.text: Middle of city centre scrapped in redevelopment, possibly?

indicators.note: redevelopment, like rebuilding a town, rearranges the letters given
the middle of the word city is its central two letters

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a city centre was torn out during urban redevelopment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Middle of' city gives IT; 'redevelopment' rearranges IT with CENTRE SCRAPPED IN into the answer. The whole clue also describes a traffic-free zone, made by redeveloping a town centre.
explanation.definitionFit: A traffic-free shopping area in the middle of a town is typically created by redeveloping and closing roads in the centre.

clue.text: Country location of Biodome Project and its name

parts.note: the Eden Project, a famous biodome attraction, is in Cornwall, in the south-west of England, abbreviated SW
the biodome attraction is called the Eden Project, so its name is Eden

explanation.surface: Asking which country hosts a biodome project and what it is called.
explanation.walkthrough: The Eden Project is a giant greenhouse attraction in Cornwall, in south-west England: SW plus EDEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweden is a Scandinavian nation, so it is an example of a country.

clue.text: Signalling direction in bricklayer's work

definitions.meaning: showing which way to go by indicating with a finger
filling and finishing the mortar joints between bricks

explanation.walkthrough: In British building, finishing the mortar between bricks is a recognised trade job with its own name.
explanation.definitionFit: Indicating a way with a finger is one sense; the other is the builder's trade term for finishing mortar joints in brickwork.

clue.text: See 25
See 3
See 1
During send-off, show idle characters, such as women of leisure

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go during, that is inside, the word for send-off

parts.note: a launch is a send-off, as of a ship

indicators.note: the characters, or letters, of the two words are reshuffled, taken as an arrangement of their letters

explanation.surface: At a farewell party, idle people show up, the sort of leisured women who have time on their hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'show' and 'idle' read as a lazy display, but 'characters' asks for those words' letters to be reshuffled; 'During' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a stock British idiom for well-off women with time to meet for long midday meals, a picture of leisure.

clue.text: Test we hear? A river

parts.note: the Ural is a river flowing through Russia and Kazakhstan

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a river is something we hear tested.
explanation.walkthrough: In British music exams the listening test is called an aural, a noun as well as an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A music examination component testing listening skills is called by this name, being concerned with hearing.

clue.text: I haven't cut up on motorway in colourless environment? I probably have!

indicators.note: the inner letters are placed in the outer word
the word for colourless forms the surroundings, the environment, of the rest

parts.note: wan means pale or colourless

indicators.note: cut up signals the letters of the words are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for motorway, as in the M1

explanation.surface: A driver denies cutting anyone up on the motorway in a pale setting, while an aside admits they probably did.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut up' anagrams I HAVEN'T, and 'in' and 'environment' place it with M inside a word for pale. Drivers of unmarked white vans have a British reputation for aggressive driving, hence the confession.
explanation.definitionFit: The stereotype of an aggressive British van driver is someone likely to have cut others up on the road, so the exclamation fits.

clue.text: Boy short of an idiotic case: on Pike's head it's marked "Stupid Boy"

indicators.note: short of means lacking the following word

parts.note: Duncan is a boy's name

indicators.note: idiotic suggests the letters of the word are scrambled senselessly
the head of the name is its first letter

explanation.surface: A dim lad's cap on the head of Pike, the Dad's Army character, labelled with his catchphrase.
explanation.walkthrough: In the British sitcom Dad's Army, Captain Mainwaring calls young Private Pike 'Stupid boy'. DUNCAN short of AN is DUNC; 'idiotic' rearranges CASE into ESCA; P is Pike's head.
explanation.definitionFit: A conical hat once put on slow pupils as punishment, effectively labelling the wearer foolish.

clue.text: Town fast approaching North

parts.note: presto is the musical direction for fast

explanation.surface: A town coming up quickly as you head north.
explanation.walkthrough: Preston is a town in Lancashire, in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Preston is a Lancashire settlement, so it is an example of a town.

clue.text: On this train, loco

definitions.meaning: a small child's chamber pot, used in toilet training

explanation.walkthrough: 'train' and 'loco' suggest railways, but one is toilet training and the other Spanish-derived slang for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: A toddler learns toilet habits on a little pot; and as slang the word means crazy, like loco.

clue.text: 9's 10? Almost, possibly violent

indicators.note: possibly signals the letters may be arranged differently

parts.note: the numeral 9 with its 's spelt out as a word

indicators.note: almost means the word is not quite complete, losing its final letter

parts.note: the numeral 10 spelt out

explanation.surface: Looks like a cross-reference to two other clues in the grid, nudging the solver to fetch their answers.
explanation.walkthrough: The numbers look like references to 9 and 10 across, but are the words NINE'S and TEN. 'Almost' cuts TEN to TE; 'possibly' rearranges NINESTE.
explanation.definitionFit: Intense can describe something extreme or forceful, such as violent emotion, so the two are near synonyms.

clue.text: Cringeworthy cryptic clue got in (about Hitler's bottom)

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go about, around, the next piece
cryptic means puzzling or obscure, hinting the letters are disguised by reordering

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

indicators.note: the bottom of a word in a down clue is its last letter

explanation.surface: An embarrassing crossword clue managed to sneak in a mention of a dictator's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cryptic' rearranges CLUE GOT IN, and 'about' puts that around R, the 'bottom' of Hitler's.
explanation.definitionFit: Something so embarrassing it makes your toes clench is cringeworthy, an informal synonym.

clue.text: Three rights, one heartless, make a wrong

indicators.note: make here means the pieces are put together in a new order

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right, so three of them are three Rs

indicators.note: heartless means the central letter of the word is removed

parts.note: the number spelt as a word

explanation.surface: A moral sum: several rights, one lacking heart, add up to a wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' takes the N from ONE, leaving OE, and 'make' rearranges RRR with OE. The surface plays on the saying that two wrongs don't make a right.
explanation.definitionFit: An error is a mistake, and a wrong is a mistake or misdeed, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Italian composer to dump resident, no good

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: no good means the letter G, for good, is dropped

parts.note: Stig of the Dump is a British children's novel whose hero, Stig, lives in a dump

explanation.surface: A composer from Italy is told to get rid of a useless tenant.
explanation.walkthrough: Stig of the Dump is a classic British children's book about a cave boy living in a chalk pit used as a rubbish dump. Remove G, for good, from STIG.
explanation.definitionFit: Francesco Paolo Tosti was an Italian songwriter known for salon songs, so he is an Italian composer.

clue.text: See 19 across
Common toilet — make for it!

parts.note: bog is British slang for toilet
a standard is a battle flag that troops rally to, so it is something to make for

explanation.surface: Someone spots an ordinary public toilet and urges a dash to it.
explanation.walkthrough: BOG is British slang for a toilet; a STANDARD is the regimental flag soldiers head for when rallying.
explanation.definitionFit: Bog-standard is British slang for basic or ordinary, so it means common.

clue.text: Bend put straight inside which to rule sheets

indicators.note: the second piece is placed inside the first
putting the word straight means sorting its letters into a new order

parts.note: to rule is to draw a line, as on paper

explanation.surface: Straightening a bend in a ruled line, like the creases in bed sheets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bend' looks like the verb, but 'put straight' sorts its letters so that a word for ruling can sit 'inside which'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bed linen is the collective name for sheets and pillowcases, so sheets are an example of it.

clue.text: Log on Kirk's star-ship only half complete

indicators.note: only half complete means the second half of the word is lost, keeping five of ten letters

parts.note: Captain Kirk commands the starship Enterprise in Star Trek

explanation.surface: Logging on to Captain Kirk's starship, which is only half built.
explanation.walkthrough: The Enterprise is the starship of Captain Kirk in Star Trek; only its first half is used.
explanation.definitionFit: To log on is to enter a computer system, signing in to it.

clue.text: Desired for rejection of reject, noted discrimination admitted

indicators.note: admitted means let inside the other piece
rejection here means the word is turned back on itself

parts.note: to deny is to reject
an ear, as in an ear for music, is the ability to discriminate between notes

explanation.surface: A bureaucratic sentence about wanting to overturn a refusal on grounds of discrimination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejection of' turns the word for reject back to front, giving YNED, and 'admitted' takes in the second piece. An ear is a musical talent for telling notes apart.
explanation.definitionFit: Yearned means longed for, so it is a synonym of desired.

clue.text: A brief question about 4 leaves you trembling

indicators.note: about means the shortened word goes around the number
brief means the word is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: a query is a question
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A short question about a reference to another clue leaves the solver shaking.
explanation.walkthrough: '4' looks like a reference to 4 down but is just a Roman numeral, which 'about' wraps the 'brief' question around; 'leaves you' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Aquiver means quivering or shaking, so it is a synonym of trembling.

clue.text: A toilet for spies

parts.note: the gents is the British term for a men's public toilet

explanation.surface: A toilet set aside for secret agents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The gents' is the British name for a men's public toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Agents are operatives working for an intelligence service, so they are spies.

clue.text: See 11
Alkaline compound of unstable character absorbing shortfall on the side

indicators.note: absorbing means the first piece takes the others inside it

parts.note: Mr Hyde is the dark alter ego of Dr Jekyll, an unstable character
fall is drop, and short makes it lose its last letter
a side is a team of eleven, XI in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A chemistry note about an alkali whose unstable nature absorbs a side deficit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortfall' is read as short fall: DROP missing its last letter, DRO, placed on XI, a cricket or football side of eleven. HYDE is the evil half of Jekyll and Hyde.
explanation.definitionFit: A hydroxide is a chemical compound containing the hydroxide ion, and many such compounds are alkaline bases.

clue.text: See 1
Place too high a price on the speed of deliveries?

definitions.text: Place too high a price on
definitions.meaning: to value something more than it deserves
in cricket, the ... at which a team bowls its ..., deliveries being balls bowled

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a delivery is one ball bowled and six make an over, so the speed of deliveries is the cricket over rate; 'deliveries' looks like post or parcels.
explanation.definitionFit: To set too high a value is to inflate a price; in cricket, the speed of bowling overs is measured as a rate.

clue.text: See 9
Lean part of the foot

definitions.meaning: to tilt over, as a ship ... in the wind
the back part of the foot below the ankle

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lean' looks like an adjective meaning thin but is the sailing verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship heeling over leans to one side; and the rounded rear of the foot is its anatomical name.

clue.text: From 4 or Senegal? The former, perhaps?

indicators.note: from points to letters taken from within the run of words that follows

parts.note: 4 is the answer to 4 down, a Scandinavian country, followed by the words or Senegal

explanation.surface: Asking whether something comes from one of two countries, and suggesting it is the first.
explanation.walkthrough: The 4 is replaced by its answer, a country, then the answer is found across the end of that country's name and the words 'or Senegal'. 'The former' points to the first of the two countries.
explanation.definitionFit: Norse means relating to Scandinavia, so something from the former, Scandinavian, country might be so described.

clue.text: Make allowances for endless stretch at university at conclusion of course

indicators.note: endless means the final letter of the word is removed

parts.note: to extend is to stretch
taken as written

indicators.note: the conclusion of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: Excusing a long stint at university that only ends when the course does.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' cuts EXTEND to EXTEN; add U, AT and E, the 'conclusion of' course.
explanation.definitionFit: To extenuate is to lessen the seriousness of a fault by offering excuses, so to make allowances for it.
